main.title: Ridge Racer 6
main.summary: Ridge Racer 6 is a 2005 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the Xbox 360.

cards.heading: Ridge Racer joins the Xbox 360 launch
cards.text: Ridge Racer 6 is a 2005 racing video game developed and published by Namco for the Xbox 360. It is an installment in the Ridge Racer series. Unlike the previous mainline entries, which were released for either PlayStation or Nintendo consoles, this entry was released exclusively as a launch title for the Xbox 360 in 2005, marking the series' debut on Xbox consoles, while a European release followed in January 2006 through a co-publishing agreement with Electronic Arts.

cards.heading: Namco's last entry before the merger
cards.text: Ridge Racer 6 was the last game in the series made while Namco remained an independent company, before its 2006 merger with Bandai's games division. Ridge Racer 7 followed on PlayStation 3. In November 2021, the Xbox twentieth-anniversary backwards compatibility update made Ridge Racer 6 playable on Xbox One and Xbox Series X/S.

main.title: Animal Crossing: Wild World
main.summary: Animal Crossing: Wild World is a 2005 social simulation video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS handheld game console.

cards.text: Animal Crossing: Wild World is a 2005 social simulation video game developed and published by Nintendo for the Nintendo DS handheld game console. It was released in Japan in November 2005, in North America and Australia in December 2005, and in Europe in March 2006. It is the second installment in the Animal Crossing series, and the sequel to Animal Crossing on the GameCube.

Wild World focuses on living in a remote village populated with anthropomorphic animals, where the player character is encouraged to perform a number of tasks, such as collecting and planting. Like all Animal Crossing titles, the game is synced to the console's clock and calendar, allowing the game to be played in real-time, which affects the occurrence of in-game events based on the current time of day or season. Wild World utilized Nintendo Wi-Fi Connection, which allowed players to travel and visit the villages of other players via online play, until the service was shut down in May 2014.

The game received positive reviews upon release, garnering aggregate scores of 86/100 on Metacritic and GameRankings. Wild World is the ninth best-selling game on the Nintendo DS with 11.75 million copies sold worldwide as of March 31, 2016. It was additionally re-released on the Wii U Virtual Console in October 2016.

main.title: Mario & Luigi: Partners in Time
main.subtitle: The brothers meet themselves
main.summary: Mario & Luigi: Partners in Time is AlphaDream's Nintendo DS role-playing adventure about a rescue across the Mushroom Kingdom's past and present. Mario and Luigi meet their infant selves while following Princess Peach into a conflict with the invading Shroobs. The four heroes travel together, but their different sizes and abilities allow them to separate when a route requires it. The comedy comes from seeing the brothers confront another version of themselves; the game turns that same idea into a practical arrangement for exploration and combat.

cards.heading: The brothers meet themselves
cards.text: Mario & Luigi: Partners in Time is AlphaDream's Nintendo DS role-playing adventure about a rescue across the Mushroom Kingdom's past and present. Mario and Luigi meet their infant selves while following Princess Peach into a conflict with the invading Shroobs. The four heroes travel together, but their different sizes and abilities allow them to separate when a route requires it. The comedy comes from seeing the brothers confront another version of themselves; the game turns that same idea into a practical arrangement for exploration and combat.

cards.heading: Four buttons for four travellers
cards.text: Each hero is associated with a face button, extending the series' timed actions from a pair of brothers to a group of four. Battles remain turn-based, but well-timed inputs strengthen attacks and help the characters respond to incoming blows. The player must recognise which member of the party needs to act. That relationship makes the team tangible through the controls: the babies are not simply additional portraits in a menu. Their presence asks for another layer of coordination during otherwise familiar jumps, hammers and defensive actions.

cards.heading: A smaller route through the world
cards.text: Adults and babies can split up, letting the younger pair reach places the older brothers cannot. The DS screens help keep the separated groups visible, while the ordinary travelling view uses the upper screen for a map. Progress depends on bringing these different routes back into the same objective. AlphaDream builds its time-travel premise into the player's handling of space: the same character can be large or small, and a barrier for one version becomes an invitation to hand the next action to the other.

main.title: Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones
main.subtitle: The return to Babylon
main.summary: Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones returned the Prince to Babylon in December 2005, concluding the trilogy begun by The Sands of Time. Ubisoft Montreal’s action adventure appeared on PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube and Windows. His homecoming with Kaileena leads into a city at war and a struggle against a darker version of himself.

cards.heading: The return to Babylon
cards.text: Prince of Persia: The Two Thrones returned the Prince to Babylon in December 2005, concluding the trilogy begun by The Sands of Time. Ubisoft Montreal’s action adventure appeared on PlayStation 2, Xbox, GameCube and Windows. His homecoming with Kaileena leads into a city at war and a struggle against a darker version of himself.

cards.heading: Two forms of the same Prince
cards.text: Acrobatic routes across walls and rooftops meet a new Speed Kill system, which rewards approaching an opponent unseen and striking at the right moment. The Dark Prince changes the rhythm with his bladed chain and different abilities. The two playable forms turn the conflict within the protagonist into changes in movement and combat.

cards.heading: Closing the trilogy
cards.text: Outdoor districts, interiors and chariot sequences make Babylon more than a destination at the end of the journey. The game brings the trilogy’s movement, fighting and manipulation of time back into the same urban setting. Its score combines contributions from Stuart Chatwood and Inon Zur, connecting the adventure to the musical identity of its predecessors.

main.title: Dragon Quest Heroes: Rocket Slime
main.subtitle: The slime becomes the adventurer
main.summary: Dragon Quest Heroes: Rocket Slime is Tose's Nintendo DS action adventure starring Rocket, one of the familiar Slimes from Dragon Quest. His home of Boingburg has been attacked, and rescuing its inhabitants sends him through areas populated by the series' recognisable monsters. The adventure alternates overhead exploration with battles between enormous tanks. Its elastic hero supplies the connection between them: objects gathered during an excursion can become ammunition in the next confrontation. The small creature normally encountered by beginning adventurers becomes the resourceful centre of his own rescue mission.

cards.heading: The slime becomes the adventurer
cards.text: Dragon Quest Heroes: Rocket Slime is Tose's Nintendo DS action adventure starring Rocket, one of the familiar Slimes from Dragon Quest. His home of Boingburg has been attacked, and rescuing its inhabitants sends him through areas populated by the series' recognisable monsters. The adventure alternates overhead exploration with battles between enormous tanks. Its elastic hero supplies the connection between them: objects gathered during an excursion can become ammunition in the next confrontation. The small creature normally encountered by beginning adventurers becomes the resourceful centre of his own rescue mission.

cards.heading: Bounce an object and catch it
cards.text: Rocket's Elasto Blast charges a forward launch that strikes an enemy or object and sends it into the air. Moving beneath it allows Rocket to catch and carry it, with room for a small stack of items or creatures. Throwing provides another way to use what has been collected. Railway carts carry rescued Slimes and other discoveries back to Boingburg, linking exploration with the town's gradual recovery. The basic movement therefore supports fighting, gathering and rescuing, giving a simple elastic charge several useful consequences inside the same scene.

cards.heading: A collection becomes ammunition
cards.text: Tank battles move the action inside a mobile fortress, where collected objects are loaded into cannons and launched toward the opponent. The stock gathered while exploring becomes a practical resource, making the earlier choice to carry something home matter in a different kind of encounter. Rescuing Boingburg's inhabitants also brings new helpers and information back to the town. The two halves of the adventure continually support each other: a short outing produces people and supplies, and the next tank fight asks how well those discoveries can be put to work.

main.title: Battles of Prince of Persia
main.subtitle: Commanding armies instead of acrobatics
main.summary: Battles of Prince of Persia is Ubisoft Montreal’s 2005 strategy spin-off for Nintendo DS.

cards.heading: Commanding armies instead of acrobatics
cards.text: Battles of Prince of Persia is Ubisoft Montreal’s 2005 strategy spin-off for Nintendo DS. Its North American release is dated December 6, while Nintendo’s British product page records December 8. Set between The Sands of Time and Warrior Within, it follows the consequences of the Prince’s efforts to escape the Dahaka: an ancient evil is unleashed and Persia and India are drawn into war. Rather than guide a lone acrobat through traps, players command armies and follow several generals. The touchscreen becomes a battlefield, while the other screen supplies information and battle scenes. The shift changes the series’ familiar struggle against time into a problem of orders, resources and positioning.

cards.heading: Cards, terrain and changing allegiances
cards.text: Cards determine what an army can do. Some issue movement and attack orders; others alter the conditions of a confrontation, so a useful hand must be considered alongside terrain, unit strengths and the opposing force. Battles are organised into turns within larger hours, making the sequence of actions important. The campaign changes perspective among Persia, India and the Daeva. Multiplayer extends the card-and-board approach, including a hot-seat option on one system. Stuart Chatwood composed the music, with a separate team credited for the music-and-game mix.

main.title: Metal Gear Acid 2
main.subtitle: A brighter look for a careful plan
main.summary: Metal Gear Acid 2 is Konami's PSP tactical card game, first released in Japan on 8 December 2005. It continues Acid's alternate Metal Gear continuity, using cards to determine movement and actions during a turn-based stealth mission. A new cel-shaded presentation gives the sequel a much brighter appearance than its predecessor. The change is visual rather than a rejection of the central idea: the player still prepares a deck, reads the current hand and decides how to cross a guarded space with the resources that have become available.

cards.heading: A brighter look for a careful plan
cards.text: Metal Gear Acid 2 is Konami's PSP tactical card game, first released in Japan on 8 December 2005. It continues Acid's alternate Metal Gear continuity, using cards to determine movement and actions during a turn-based stealth mission. A new cel-shaded presentation gives the sequel a much brighter appearance than its predecessor. The change is visual rather than a rejection of the central idea: the player still prepares a deck, reads the current hand and decides how to cross a guarded space with the resources that have become available.

cards.heading: Let the partner support the attack
cards.text: New cover-fire behaviour allows an ally in a suitable position to support an attack, making coordination useful alongside the strength of an individual card. Surplus cards can be sold, giving deck management another way to improve the collection. Movement also becomes smoother around doors and items, reducing interruptions while retaining the turn-based decisions. The player has to think about where both characters stand before committing to a confrontation. A powerful card becomes more valuable when the surrounding positions allow the partner to contribute instead of leaving the attacker isolated.

cards.heading: A cardboard viewer adds another dimension
cards.text: The release included Solid Eye, a folding cardboard accessory whose lenses turn a divided PSP image into a stereoscopic view. It gives the game's unusual presentation a physical counterpart, inviting the player to look into the handheld differently. Shinta Nojiri returned as director, with music by Akihiro Honda, Hiroshi Tanabe and Nobuko Toda. Western editions followed in 2006. Acid 2 develops a small but distinctive branch of Metal Gear, combining familiar espionage imagery with deck construction, measured movement and an accessory unlike the ordinary equipment attached to a portable console.

main.title: Rogue Galaxy
main.subtitle: Leave the home planet behind
main.summary: Rogue Galaxy is Level-5's PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 8 December 2005. Jaster Rogue begins as a young agricultural worker on an isolated planet before becoming involved with a spacefaring crew and a conflict that reaches across the galaxy. The adventure turns his wish for a wider life into a sequence of new worlds and companions. Exploration leads directly into active battles, keeping the journey close to the characters on screen. Its scale reflects Level-5's ambition to build a large original role-playing adventure for Sony's console.

cards.heading: Leave the home planet behind
cards.text: Rogue Galaxy is Level-5's PlayStation 2 action role-playing game, first released in Japan on 8 December 2005. Jaster Rogue begins as a young agricultural worker on an isolated planet before becoming involved with a spacefaring crew and a conflict that reaches across the galaxy. The adventure turns his wish for a wider life into a sequence of new worlds and companions. Exploration leads directly into active battles, keeping the journey close to the characters on screen. Its scale reflects Level-5's ambition to build a large original role-playing adventure for Sony's console.

cards.heading: Give the crew reasons to keep exploring
cards.text: Real-time combat allows the player to move and attack while companions take part around the controlled character. Character development and equipment provide work between encounters, while numerous optional activities extend the journey beyond the next story destination. A planet can therefore offer both a place in the main adventure and something worth returning to later. The structure encourages the player to treat the crew as an ongoing group whose abilities and equipment continue to develop. Progress is expressed through those preparations as well as the discovery of another part of the galaxy.

cards.heading: A larger edition travels overseas
cards.text: Akihiro Hino and Takeshi Akasaka directed the project, with Tomohito Nishiura composing its music. Development lasted more than three years and involved a larger team than Level-5 had previously used. An expanded Director's Cut became the basis of the 2007 North American and PAL releases, adding changes beyond the first Japanese edition. Reviewers praised the presentation and range of activities while responding less uniformly to the story and characters. The game brought Level-5's experience with expansive console adventures into an original space-fantasy setting, combining a long journey with many smaller diversions.

main.title: Yakuza
main.subtitle: A district small enough to become home
main.summary: On December 8, 2005, SEGA released Ryū ga Gotoku for PlayStation 2 in Japan, the game that would reach the West as Yakuza.

cards.heading: Kiryu enters Kamurocho
cards.text: Yakuza is SEGA's PlayStation 2 crime adventure following Kazuma Kiryu through the compact district of Kamurocho. Close-range fighting sits alongside restaurants, arcades, shops and encounters with people on the street. Its main story uses betrayal, money and family loyalties to build a crime melodrama, while side stories make room for comedy and everyday problems. The game first appeared in Japan as Ry? ga Gotoku on December 8, 2005.

cards.heading: Learning the district on foot
cards.text: Shops, alleys, signs, restaurants and arcades give Kamurocho recognisable landmarks. Walking between them brings interruptions and side stories as well as the next destination in the main plot. Repeated visits help the player learn intersections and shortcuts through use. The series' later returns to the district build on that familiarity, letting a changed shop or relationship stand out against the place players remember.

cards.heading: Picking up a weapon from the street
cards.text: Kiryu can strike, grab and pick up objects during a street fight. Bicycles, signs and other nearby objects become weapons, giving the surroundings a practical role in an encounter. Character growth supplies new techniques, while substories also award experience. Exploring the district and helping its residents can therefore contribute to the abilities Kiryu brings into the next brawl.

cards.heading: Clan drama and ordinary people
cards.text: The main plot revolves around clans, betrayal, money and family bonds. Its crime drama gives Kiryu responsibilities that carry weight across the story. Encounters on the street can then interrupt that intensity with requests or small deceptions. The player moves between these registers while continuing to inhabit the same district, seeing how Kiryu responds to both serious conflicts and ordinary people.

cards.heading: SEGA addresses an adult audience
cards.text: SEGA presented Ry? ga Gotoku as entertainment for adults. Writer Hase Seishu supervised the script, and well-known actors joined the voice cast. Money, nightlife, hierarchies and loyalty gave the contemporary Japanese setting its social world. Familiar game activities, including fights and minigames, supplied ways to take part in it. The combination helped establish the series' particular balance of local detail and accessible action.

cards.heading: The first Western release
cards.text: Yakuza reached North America on September 5, 2006, following the Japanese release of Ry? ga Gotoku in December 2005. The same first adventure introduced Western players to Kiryu and Kamurocho. Travelling on foot made the district's restaurants, arcades, bars and alleys part of the routine between scenes. The series began overseas with the same mixture of criminal melodrama and smaller encounters.

cards.heading: Arcade and console developers build a new kind of game
cards.text: Yakuza's team included developers with backgrounds in Virtua Fighter 3, Super Monkey Ball, Panzer Dragoon and Jet Set Radio. The team members all felt that the new game didn't match anything they had previously done. Producer Toshihiro Nagoshi felt that this was an advantage, putting them all on an even playing field. Anything that was done had to go through Nagoshi first, since only he had a concrete idea of how the game would turn out.

cards.heading: Finding Kiryu in the side stories
cards.text: Side stories give Kiryu occasions to deal with people beyond the central criminal conflict. A request may lead to a ridiculous situation, a small deception or an everyday problem. These encounters help establish his personality through the way he responds. Their optional place in the journey allows a different tone to emerge before the player returns to the more urgent main story.

cards.heading: The spectacle of a Heat move
cards.text: The Heat system gives Kiryu spectacular moves that underline his strength during a fight. Close-range encounters can leave him outnumbered, drawing attention to the force of those attacks. Once a battle ends, he returns to walking through Kamurocho. That immediate return keeps the district familiar as both the scene of violence and the setting for food, games and conversations.

main.title: Mega Man Maverick Hunter X
main.subtitle: X returns with another way into the story
main.summary: Mega Man Maverick Hunter X is Capcom's PSP action-platform game, first released in Japan on 15 December 2005. It rebuilds the original Mega Man X with three-dimensional graphics while retaining side-on stages and the search for weapons gained from defeated bosses. X confronts Sigma and the Mavericks, with added story material giving his relationships more context. The player still chooses which stage to attempt and gradually expands the tools available for the rest. The remake offers both a return to familiar routes and another playable perspective through the rival character Vile.

cards.heading: X returns with another way into the story
cards.text: Mega Man Maverick Hunter X is Capcom's PSP action-platform game, first released in Japan on 15 December 2005. It rebuilds the original Mega Man X with three-dimensional graphics while retaining side-on stages and the search for weapons gained from defeated bosses. X confronts Sigma and the Mavericks, with added story material giving his relationships more context. The player still chooses which stage to attempt and gradually expands the tools available for the rest. The remake offers both a return to familiar routes and another playable perspective through the rival character Vile.

cards.heading: A new weapon changes a familiar obstacle
cards.text: Eight principal stages provide bosses whose powers become part of X's equipment. Choosing their order allows the player to experiment with which acquired ability helps against the next opponent or section. Movement and attack remain closely connected, as a safe position can matter as much as the weapon selected. The alternative Vile mode changes the available arsenal and the approach to those spaces. Returning knowledge therefore has to be tested rather than applied automatically, because another character's capabilities can make a familiar encounter ask for a different solution.

cards.heading: Rebuild the beginning instead of adding a ninth game
cards.text: The team considered a new Mega Man X sequel before choosing to revisit the original for PSP. Kazuki Matsue directed the project, with Tatsuya Yoshikawa contributing its visual design and a new score credited to Kento Hasegawa, Seiko Kobuchi and Shinya Okada. Voice acting and The Day of Sigma animated prequel expand the presentation around the action. North American and European releases followed in 2006. These additions make Maverick Hunter X a substantial reinterpretation, using a familiar foundation to explore the series' opening from another visual and narrative angle.
